claims.text: The initial equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy has a simple crystal structure.
Adding a controlled amount of carbon to CoCrFeNiTi through powder metallurgy will improve hardness.
Adding a controlled amount of carbon to CoCrFeNiTi through powder metallurgy will improve its mechanical performance.
Carbon modification will preserve the favorable plasticity of CoCrFeNiTi.
Carbon modification will preserve the favorable machinability of CoCrFeNiTi.
Subsequent heat treatment will homogenize the powder-metallurgy-processed alloy.
Subsequent heat treatment will produce precipitation hardening in the carbon-modified alloy.
Carbon addition will cause carbide precipitates to form in CoCrFeNiTi.
Carbide precipitates will act as obstacles to dislocation movement.
Obstructing dislocation movement through precipitates will strengthen the alloy.
Precipitation hardening will enhance hardness and broader mechanical performance.
The carbon-modified alloy will have at least 15% greater hardness than the unmodified alloy.
The carbon-modified alloy will have at least 10% greater yield strength than the unmodified alloy.
The carbon-modified alloy will retain at least 5% elongation at break.
The proposed effect applies for processing temperatures from 1000°C to 1200°C.
The proposed mechanical-property effects apply over testing temperatures from 25°C to 600°C.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires at least 15% higher hardness and 10% higher yield strength, but the stated falsification rule only requires 10% and 5%, respectively. Results between these thresholds would fail the prediction without falsifying the hypothesis under the specified rule.
The hypothesis claims preservation of machinability, but the experiment includes no machinability measurement or associated falsification criterion.
